summary:
Visitors to Bauchi State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public displays of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and Human Rights Watch has documented police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. On top of that, Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force: the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms the religious penal codes of all twelve northern Nigerian states, Bauchi among them, and records male sodomy as carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Bauchi is the one state where that capital ceiling has actually been pronounced for same-sex conduct. On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna, to death by stoning for homosexuality, holding that they violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through their lawyer Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested committing the offence at Gwada village on 14 June 2022. Reuters reported it on 2 July 2022 as the first time the death penalty had been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The presiding judge, Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi, granted a 30-day appeal window, and the UK Home Office note records that the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor. Relatives told Punch, which published on 16 July 2022, that the judgment had not been carried out at that point. A further report cited in the same Home Office note placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Bauchi Sharia court in May 2024.

Courtrooms in Bauchi have themselves been targets of mob pressure. At a sodomy trial in January 2014 at the Tudun Alkali Upper Sharia Court in Bauchi, an angry mob stormed the premises demanding a death sentence. Against that, appellate courts in the state have overturned capital sodomy convictions: Amnesty International's 2004 press release records that the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed Jubrin Babaji's death-by-stoning sentence, convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, for denial of counsel and a defective confession, following the quashing of Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction on 14 November 2003, and describes a number of cases in which convictions and death sentences were quashed on appeal.

Gender expression, not identity, is the trigger for arrest in Bauchi. Eighteen men were arrested by Bauchi state police and charged with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code; the charges were later reduced to vagrancy and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial before the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011. Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held under Shari'a charges for years. Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Violence risk outside the courts is high and documented nationally. The Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in April 2024 on kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a direct hazard for a visitor using dating apps. Police extortion accompanies enforcement: in March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded for looking gay. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and The Dial recorded in February 2025 that six months later no suspects had been charged.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Bauchi's record is extreme within Nigeria but not isolated: the death-by-stoning sentence pronounced here in 2022 sits inside a twelve-state zone of religious criminal law, and the national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act supplies a secular ceiling of 14 years' imprisonment that applies in every state regardless of which code prosecutes.

The 2022 Ningi sentence is distinguished from earlier Bauchi capital cases by outcome rather than by charge. Babaji and Chiyawa were both convicted under the same state penal code and both had their convictions quashed on appeal in 2003 and 2004; the 2022 sentences were pronounced with an appeal window and a governor's ratification requirement attached, and no execution is recorded.

Prison placement for trans detainees in Nigeria has been left to official discretion rather than rule. Press coverage of Bobrisky's (Idris Okuneye) sentencing in April 2024 openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in; she served her six-month naira-abuse sentence in a maximum-security prison in Lagos, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her there violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender, while dismissing bribery allegations.

Enforcement in Bauchi has historically been driven by non-state complainants as much as by police: the 2022 prosecution was brought by the Hisbah Vanguard, and the 2014 disturbance at the Tudun Alkali court involved a mob demanding a sentence rather than the bench imposing one.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bauchi State live under the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 alongside the federal criminal statutes, and Section 133 and Section 134 of that code supply the sodomy and homosexuality offences used in the stoning prosecutions. The state's own courts have handed down the sentences; the state governor holds the ratification power over whether a death sentence is carried out.

The eighteen men held for dressing as women were charged first with sodomy and then with vagrancy, and remained in jail for several years awaiting trial, with the detention ending only by the close of 2011. That sequence shows the practical path a gender-nonconforming resident faces: arrest on a Shari'a charge, reduction to a minor offence, and prolonged pre-trial custody.

Bobrisky's case is the country's most prominent example of a trans woman passing through the prison system. Sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months' imprisonment without the option of a fine for four counts of naira abuse, she was held in a maximum-security facility in Lagos and released on 5 August 2024; the October 2024 panel found that placement breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act for a first-time offender.

Appellate relief is available and has been used in Bauchi. The Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed a death-by-stoning sodomy conviction in 2004 on the grounds that the accused was denied counsel and that the confession was defective, one of a number of such quashings on appeal recorded by Amnesty International.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the death-by-stoning sentences pronounced at Ningi in June 2022 were ratified by the Bauchi State governor, appealed successfully, or carried out is unresolved in the sources assembled here; the last dated account records them as not carried out and subject to a 30-day appeal window.

The status of the reported May 2024 death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Bauchi Sharia court is unresolved: no follow-up on appeal, ratification or execution is sourced.

Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted into law is not settled by the available sources.

No source records where trans-feminine detainees in Bauchi are housed inside custody, whether in a male or female wing, a special unit, or solitary confinement, and no trans-specific placement rule, facility or policy for Bauchi is documented.

The number of the eighteen men eventually convicted, the precise dates of their release, and whether any compensation followed remain not sourced.
